I need to think through this season as a 65-year-old highly educated cotton farmer with 12 mu and 40 years of experience.

**My thinking as the farmer:**

I'm getting older now—65—and it's just my wife and me managing these 12 mu of cotton. I've been farming this land for 40 years, so I know every corner of these fields. The soil here is reasonably fertile, but I've learned that cotton is hungry, especially during flowering and boll-setting. With my education background, I understand the principles—nitrogen drives vegetative growth but too much makes the plants tall and hollow, phosphorus helps root development, potassium is critical for boll weight and fiber quality. But I'm also practical. I can't afford to over-apply because input prices keep rising, and at my age, I need to preserve cash for medical expenses and hired labor during picking season.

This year, I'm targeting about 280 kg of lint per mu. That's realistic if the weather cooperates—I've hit 300 before in good years, but last year was only around 250 because of a dry August. I'll plant around April 20th, once the soil temperature at 5 cm stays above 14°C consistently. I'll use an improved hybrid variety—probably a Bt cotton with good resistance to bollworm and Fusarium wilt. I buy certified seed every year; saved seed loses hybrid vigor, and I'm educated enough to know that the 200 yuan per mu for good seed pays for itself.

For fertilizer, I'll apply a base dressing before planting: about 20 kg of compound fertilizer (15-15-15) per mu, which gives me roughly 3 kg N, 3 kg P₂O₅, and 3 kg K₂O. Then at flowering—around early July—I'll topdress with 15 kg of urea per mu, adding another 7 kg N. I'll do a second topdress at peak boll-setting with another 10 kg urea if the plants look vigorous. Total N should come to around 15-17 kg/mu. I might also spray some foliar potassium at boll-opening if the leaves show deficiency. I split applications because cotton has a long growing season and leaching happens when we get those summer thunderstorms.

Irrigation: I'll irrigate three times. First, a light pre-planting irrigation in mid-April if the spring is dry, to ensure germination. The critical one is at flowering in early July—without water then, boll shedding jumps by 20%. The third is in late August if it's dry, to help boll filling. Each irrigation costs about 30-40 yuan/mu for pumping, so roughly 100 yuan/mu total. It's expensive but necessary.

Pesticides: With Bt cotton, I don't spray much for bollworm anymore, but I still need herbicide—I'll apply acetochlor pre-emergence for weed control. If weeds break through, I'll do one manual hoeing before the cotton gets too tall. I'll watch for aphids and spider mites; if they show up, I'll spray once, maybe twice. I'll also do one preventive fungicide application at the seedling stage because Fusarium wilt has been a problem in this area.

Tillage: I'll do shallow rotary tillage in early April to break the winter crust, then create raised beds with plastic mulch. The plastic mulch is non-negotiable for me—it warms the soil for early germination, suppresses weeds, and reduces evaporation. I hire a machine for bed-making and mulching; I can't do that physically anymore at my age.

Labor is my biggest constraint. My wife and I can handle day-to-day management—fertilizer application, irrigation monitoring, spraying—but cotton picking is back-breaking work, and at 65, my knees and back won't handle bending for 12 mu. I'll hire labor for the three to four rounds of picking from September through October. That'll cost me, but I have no choice. Family labor will be about 45 days across the season; hired labor around 35 days, mostly concentrated in picking.

My total input cost will be roughly: seed (200 × 12 = 2,400), fertilizer (base 180 × 12 = 2,160, topdress 120 × 12 = 1,440), irrigation (100 × 12 = 1,200), pesticides (80 × 12 = 960), plastic mulch and bed-making (150 × 12 = 1,800), hired labor (100 × 35 = 3,500). Total around 13,460 yuan. That's a significant outlay for a 12-mu farm, but at 280 kg/mu lint and current cotton prices around 16 yuan/kg, gross revenue would be about 53,760 yuan. After inputs and hired labor, there's still decent margin, but I have to manage cash flow carefully—I pay for inputs upfront but don't get revenue until October-November.
